newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president names new premier in reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president names new premier in reshuffle.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam, seeking to restore his political fortunes following a loans scandal, on Tuesday appointed a new prime minister with a reputation for political integrity.
Koh Kun, 59, was a mayor of Seoul from 1988-90 under former president Roh Tae-woo, but quit the post after a row with Roh's administration involving a corrupt land deal.

Koh currently is head of Myongji University. He would replace premier Lee Soo-sung after the appointment is approved by the National Assembly, a spokesman for the presidential Blue House, Yoon Yeo-joon, said.
Parliament's approval is almost certain since opposition parties have indicated full support for Koh, who had been widely tipped for the job.
Kim has launched a major reshuffle of his administration aimed at restoring his reputation badly tarnished by a scandal involving loans to failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Last week he replaced his chief secretary and three other top Blue House aides.
A cabinet reshuffle, involving key economic ministries, is widely expected this week.
Koh had extensive cabinet experience during the 1980-1988 administration of former president Chun Doo Hwan.
His reputation for integrity stems from an earlier scandal involving the Hanbo Group.
As Seoul mayor he resisted pressure from central government to rezone land for a huge public housing development by South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate.
Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo was found guilty in 1991 of bribing government officials in connection with the housing deal and was jailed for six months.

Chung is now in custody facing charges of bribery and embezzlement following an investigation into how Hanbo Steel managed to wring $5.8 billion from the banking system for an unprofitable new steel mill.
State prosecutors have accused leading politicians of influence-peddling.
Kim apologised last Tuesday over the Hanbo affair.
Former presidents Chun and Roh are both in jail after convictions for bribery and other abuses while in office.
Koh is a former minister of Home Affairs, Transportation, Agriculture and Forestry. He took up his university post in 1994.
Koh was born in Seoul. His family hails from Cholla province, a traditional hotbed of opposition politics.

Cholla residents believe their poor southwest province has been deprived as punishment for opposition to central government, whose leaders are overwhelmingly from wealthy Kyongsang province next door.
Koh was governor of South Cholla province in 1979.
Kim has come under fire from opposition parties for packing his administration more than usual with fellow Kyongsang natives.
The opposition claims this has bred incompetence and influence-peddling.
Current prime minister Lee, an eminent legal scholar, was plucked from the presidency of Seoul National University by Kim in 1995.
